source_text: Si, quod iniquitas a deo non est, sed a diabolo, persecutio autem ex iniquitate consistit (quid enim iniquius, quam veri dei antistites, omnes sectatores veritatis nocentissimorum more tractari?), ideo videtur persecutio a diabolo evenire, a quo iniquitas agitur ex qua constat persecutio, scire debemus, quatinus nec persecutio est sine iniquitate diaboli nec probatio fidei sine persecutione, propter probationem fidei necessariam iniquitatem non patrocinium praestare persecutioni, sed ministerium; praecedere enim dei voluntatem circa fidei probationem, quae est ratio persecutionis, sequi autem diaboli iniquitatem ad instrumentum persecutionis, quae ratio est probationis. Nam et alias in quantum iustitiae iniquitas aemula est, in tantum materia est ad testimonia eius, cuius est aemula, ut sic iustitia in iniquitate perficiatur, quomodo virtus in infirmitate perficitur. Nam infirma mundi electa sunt a deo, ut confundantur fortia, et stulta eius, ut confundatur sapientia. Ita et iniquitas adhibetur, ut iustitia probetur confundens iniquitatem. Igitur quod ministerium non est arbitrii, sed servitii (arbitrium enim domini persecutio propter fidei probationem, ministerium autem iniquitas diaboli propter persecutionis instructionem), ita eam per diabolum, si forte, non a diabolo evenire credimus. Nihil satanae in servos dei vivi licebit, nisi permiserit dominus, ut aut ipsum destruat per fidem electorum in temptatione victricem, aut homines eius fuisse traducat qui defecerint ad illum. Habes exemplum Iob, cui diabolus nullam potuit incutere temptationem, nisi a deo accepisset potestatem, nec in substantiam quidem eius, nisi dominus, Ecce, dixisset, omnia quae sunt ei, in manu tua do, in ipsum autem ne extenderis manum. Denique nec extendit, nisi posteaquam et hoc postulanti dominus, Ecce, dixisset, trado tibi illum, tantum animam eius custodi. Sic et in apostolos facultatem temptationis postulavit non habens eam nisi ex permissu, siquidem dominus in evangelio ad Petrum, Ecce, inquit, postulavit satanas, ut cerneret vos velut frumentum, verum ego rogavi pro te, ne deficeret fides tua, id est, ne tantum diabolo permitteretur, ut fides periclitaretur. Quo ostenditur utrumque apud deum esse, et concussionem fidei et protectionem, cum utrumque ab eo petitur, concussio a diabolo, protectio a filio. Et utique cum filius dei protectionem fidei habet in sua potestate, quam a patre postulat, a quo omnem accipit potestatem in caelis et in terris, quale est, ut concussionem fidei diabolus in manu sua habeat? Sed in legitima oratione, cum dicimus ad patrem, Ne nos inducas in temptationem (quae autem maior temptatio, quam persecutio?), ab eo illam profitemur accidere a quo veniam eius deprecamur. Hoc est enim quod sequitur, Sed erue nos a maligno, id est, ne nos induxeris in temptationem, permittendo nos maligno. Tunc enim eruimur diaboli manibus, cum illi non tradimur in temptationem. Nec in porcorum gregem diaboli legio habuit potestatem, nisi eam de deo impetrasset; tantum potestatem abest ut in oves dei habeat. Possum dicere porcorum quoque setas tunc numeratas apud deum fuisse, nedum capillos sanctorum. Habere videtur diabolus propriam iam potestatem, si forte, in eos qui ad deum non pertinent, semel in stillam situlae et in pulverem areae et in salivam nationibus deputatis a deo ac per hoc diabolo expositis in vacuam quodammodo possessionem. Ceterum in domesticos dei nihil illi licet ex propria potestate, quia, quando liceat, id est ex quibus causis, exempla in scripturis signata demonstrant. Aut enim ex causa probationis conceditur ei ius temptationis provocato vel provocanti, ut in superioribus, aut ex causa reprobationis traditur ei peccator, quasi carnifici in poenam, ut Saul (Et abscessit, inquit, spiritus domini a Saule, et concutiebat eum spiritus nequam a domino et suffocabat eum), aut ex causa cohibitionis, ut apostolus refert datum sibi sudem angelum satanae, ut colaphizaretur; nec hanc speciem permitti diabolo in sanctos humiliandos per carnis vexationem, nisi simul ut et virtus tolerantiae scilicet in infirmitate perfici possit. Nam et ipse apostolus Phygellum et Hermogenem tradidit satanae, uti emendentur, ne blasphement. Vides iam et a servis dei facilius diabolum accipere potestatem; tanto abest, ut eam ex proprietate possideat.
thought_title: Persecution as God's testing, with the devil only as servant
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that persecution comes from the devil because it consists in wickedness, and he is explaining how God's will for testing faith precedes and uses the devil's wickedness as a mere instrument.
pass_a_gloss: If, because wickedness is not from God but from the devil, but persecution consists of wickedness (for what is more wicked than that the priests of the true God, all the followers of truth, should be treated in the manner of the most criminal?), therefore persecution seems to come about from the devil, from whom the wickedness is done of which persecution consists, we ought to know that, just as persecution is not without the wickedness of the devil, nor is the testing of faith without persecution, for the sake of the testing of faith the necessary wickedness does not furnish patronage to persecution, but service; for the will of God goes before concerning the testing of faith, which is the reason for persecution, but the wickedness of the devil follows as the instrument of persecution, which is the reason for testing. For also elsewhere, inasmuch as wickedness is the rival of righteousness, so far it is matter for the testimonies of that whose rival it is, so that righteousness is perfected in wickedness, just as strength is perfected in weakness. For the weak things of the world have been chosen by God, so that the strong things may be confounded, and the foolish things of his, so that wisdom may be confounded. So also wickedness is employed, so that righteousness may be tested, confounding wickedness. Therefore, because it is not a service of choice but of slavery (for persecution is the choice of the Lord because of the testing of faith, but the wickedness of the devil is the service because of the furnishing of persecution), so we believe that it comes about through the devil, if perhaps, not from the devil. Nothing will be permitted to Satan against the servants of the living God, unless the Lord permits it, either so that he may destroy him through the faith of the elect victorious in temptation, or so that he may prove that those who have fallen away to him were his men. You have the example of Job, on whom the devil could inflict no temptation, unless he had received power from God, not even on his substance, unless the Lord had said, Behold, all things that are his I give into your hand, but do not stretch out your hand against him himself. In fact he did not stretch it out, except after the Lord had said to him also requesting this, Behold, I hand him over to you, only preserve his soul. So also he sought the power of temptation against the apostles, not having it except by permission, since indeed the Lord in the gospel says to Peter, Behold, Satan has sought to sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail, that is, that so much may not be permitted to the devil, that faith may be endangered. By which it is shown that both things are with God, both the shaking of faith and the protection, since both are sought from him, the shaking from the devil, the protection from the Son. And certainly since the Son of God has the protection of faith in his own power, which he asks from the Father, from whom he receives all power in heaven and on earth, what sort of thing is it, that the devil should have the shaking of faith in his own hand? But in the prescribed prayer, when we say to the Father, Lead us not into temptation (but what greater temptation than persecution?), we confess that it happens from him from whom we pray for its removal. For this is what follows, But deliver us from the evil one, that is, do not lead us into temptation, by permitting us to the evil one. For then we are delivered from the hands of the devil, when we are not handed over to him in temptation. Nor did the legion of the devil have power over the herd of pigs, unless it had obtained it from God; so far is it from having power over the sheep of God. I can say that even the bristles of the pigs were then counted with God, much more the hairs of the saints. The devil seems to have his own power already, if perhaps, over those who do not belong to God, once for all in the drop of a bucket and in the dust of the threshing floor and in the spittle, the nations having been assigned by God and through this exposed to the devil in a possession as it were empty. But against the household of God nothing is permitted to him from his own power, because, when it is permitted, that is from what causes, the examples marked in the scriptures demonstrate. For either from the cause of testing the right of temptation is granted to him, provoked or provoking, as in the earlier cases, or from the cause of rejection the sinner is handed over to him, as to an executioner for punishment, as Saul (And the spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, it says, and an evil spirit from the Lord shook him and choked him), or from the cause of restraint, as the apostle reports that a stake was given to him, an angel of Satan, so that he might be buffeted; nor is this kind permitted to the devil for humbling the saints through the vexation of the flesh, unless at the same time so that the strength of endurance may be perfected in weakness. For also the apostle himself handed over Phygelus and Hermogenes to Satan, so that they might be corrected, lest they blaspheme. You see now that the devil receives power more easily even from the servants of God; so far is he from possessing it from his own property.

choices.why: The term denotes those who stand before God as chief ministers; 'priests' preserves the cultic office Tertullian assigns to Christian leaders.

choices.english: does not furnish patronage to persecution, but service
choices.why: The contrast between patrocinium and ministerium is central to the argument: wickedness does not defend or authorize persecution but serves it as an instrument.
rejected: does not give support to persecution, but assistance
does not advocate for persecution, but serves it

choices.english: for persecution is the choice of the Lord
choices.why: Arbitrium here means the Lord's own decision or will, contrasted with the devil's servile role; 'choice' keeps the sense of deliberate divine decision.

choices.term: in stillam situlae et in pulverem areae et in salivam
choices.english: in the drop of a bucket and in the dust of the threshing floor and in the spittle
choices.why: These are scriptural images of the nations' worthlessness before God; the literal rendering preserves the vivid contempt of the original.
rejected: a drop in a bucket, dust on the scales, spittle

choices.why: The Latin sudem means a pointed stake; rendering it literally preserves the physical image Paul uses for the thorn or splinter in his flesh.

choices.english: so that they might be corrected, lest they blaspheme
choices.why: The purpose clause is explicit in the source; keeping 'corrected' rather than 'taught' preserves the disciplinary sense of emendare.
rejected: so that they might learn not to blaspheme
so that they might be disciplined

pass_b_english: Someone may object: wickedness is not from God but from the devil, and persecution consists of wickedness. For what is more wicked than treating the priests of the true God, all the followers of truth, like the worst criminals? Therefore persecution seems to come from the devil, since the wickedness from which persecution is made is his work. But we must understand this: persecution is not without the devil's wickedness, nor is the testing of faith without persecution. The wickedness necessary for the testing of faith does not give patronage to persecution, but service. God's will concerning the testing of faith comes first; that is the reason for persecution. The devil's wickedness follows as the instrument of persecution, which is the means of testing.

For in other matters too, to the extent that wickedness is the rival of righteousness, it is the material for the testimony of the very thing it rivals, so that righteousness is perfected in wickedness just as strength is perfected in weakness. For God chose the weak things of the world to put the strong to shame, and its foolish things to put wisdom to shame (1 Corinthians 1:27). So wickedness is employed so that righteousness may be tested and put wickedness to shame.

Therefore, since this is not the service of choice but of slavery—for persecution is the choice of the Lord because of the testing of faith, while the devil's wickedness is the service because of the equipping of persecution—we believe that persecution comes through the devil, if at all, not from the devil.

Nothing will be permitted to Satan against the servants of the living God unless the Lord allows it, either to destroy Satan himself through the faith of the elect that conquers in temptation, or to expose as his own those who have fallen away to him. You have the example of Job, on whom the devil could inflict no temptation unless he had received power from God—not even against his property, unless the Lord had said, 'Behold, everything that is his I give into your hand, but do not stretch out your hand against him' (Job 1:12). And indeed he did not stretch out his hand until, when he asked for this too, the Lord said, 'Behold, I hand him over to you, only preserve his life' (Job 2:6).

So also he asked for the power to tempt the apostles, not having it except by permission, since the Lord in the Gospel says to Peter, 'Behold, Satan has asked to sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail' (Luke 22:31-32)—that is, that not so much be permitted to the devil that faith would be endangered. This shows that both things are with God: the assault on faith and its protection, since both are asked from him—the assault by the devil, the protection by the Son. And certainly, since the Son of God has the protection of faith in his own power, which he asks from the Father, from whom he receives all power in heaven and on earth, how could the devil have the assault on faith in his own hand?

But in the appointed prayer, when we say to the Father, 'Lead us not into temptation' (Matthew 6:13)—and what greater temptation is there than persecution?—we confess that it comes from him from whom we beg its pardon. For this is what follows: 'But deliver us from the evil one' (Matthew 6:13), that is, do not lead us into temptation by permitting us to the evil one. For then we are delivered from the devil's hands when we are not handed over to him in temptation.

Nor did the legion of demons have power over the herd of pigs unless it had obtained it from God; so far is it from having power over God's sheep. I can say that even the bristles of the pigs were numbered before God then, let alone the hairs of the saints. The devil seems to have his own power, if at all, over those who do not belong to God, since the nations were once reckoned by God as a drop of a bucket and the dust of the threshing floor and spittle, and through this were exposed to the devil as an empty possession, so to speak.

But against the household of God nothing is permitted to him from his own power, because when it is permitted—that is, from what causes—the examples marked in the Scriptures demonstrate. For either the right of temptation is granted to him for the cause of testing, whether he is challenged or challenges, as in the cases above; or for the cause of rejection the sinner is handed over to him, as to an executioner for punishment, as with Saul: 'And the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him and choked him' (1 Samuel 16:14). Or for the cause of restraint, as the apostle reports that a thorn was given to him, an angel of Satan, to strike him (2 Corinthians 12:7). Nor is this kind of thing permitted to the devil against the saints, to humble them through bodily affliction, unless at the same time the strength of endurance may be perfected in weakness. For the apostle himself handed over Phygelus and Hermogenes to Satan, so that they might be corrected, lest they blaspheme. You see now that the devil receives power more readily from God's servants; so far is he from possessing it as his own.
